LH-PROV-004.explanation: California requires a life insurance grace period of at least 60 days from the due date (Ins. Code 10113.71), so the policy was still in force on March 20. The insurer pays the face amount minus the overdue premium: $100,000 - $1,200 = $98,800, not the full $100,000.

LH-PROV-011.explanation: In California the free-look period is 10 to 30 days for buyers under 60 and at least 30 days for buyers 60 or older (Ins. Code 10127.9, 10127.10), so a return six days after delivery earns a full refund. No premium is forfeited during the free look.

LH-GEN-016.explanation: Concealment is withholding a known material fact, and in California concealment, whether intentional or unintentional, entitles the insurer to rescind (Ins. Code 331). Misrepresentation is making a false statement rather than staying silent.

LH-HLTH-016.question: To make federally tax-deductible contributions to a health savings account, an individual must:
LH-HLTH-016.explanation: Federal HSA eligibility requires coverage under a qualified high-deductible health plan; contributions are deductible, growth is tax-free and qualified withdrawals are tax-free under federal law. The use-it-or-lose-it rule belongs to flexible spending accounts, and HSA balances roll over.

LH-REG-005.explanation: A producer holds premiums as a fiduciary and must remit them or keep them in a separate trust account (Cal. Ins. Code 1733, 1734); mixing them with personal funds is commingling, which can lead to license discipline. No grace window makes depositing premiums in a personal account acceptable.

LH-HTYP-023.explanation: The Medigap open enrollment period lasts 6 months starting when a person is 65 and enrolled in Part B, and insurers must issue any plan they sell without regard to health (Cal. Ins. Code 10192.11(a)). California also gives existing Medigap insureds a 60-day birthday window to move to a plan with equal or lesser benefits.

LH-PROV-016.question: An insured and his primary beneficiary die in the same car crash, and no one can tell who died first. Under California's simultaneous death rule, proceeds are paid:
LH-PROV-016.explanation: California Probate Code 224 treats the insured as having survived unless clear and convincing evidence shows the beneficiary survived, so proceeds go to the contingent beneficiary or the insured's estate (community property proceeds with no other beneficiary are split as community property). A common disaster clause adds a short survival period requirement for the same purpose.

LH-LIFE-018.question: Gloria, diagnosed with a terminal illness and given 18 months to live, sells her $300,000 policy to a third party for $210,000. In industry terms, how is she treated?
LH-LIFE-018.explanation: The insured who sells a policy while terminally ill is called the viator (California's Insurance Code simply calls her the owner under a life settlement contract, Ins. Code 10113.1), and proceeds paid to a terminally ill seller are generally income tax-free. A healthy senior selling in a life settlement, by contrast, may owe tax on the gain.

excluded.LH-LIFE-001: Divorce case. California Probate Code 5040 makes a revocable nonprobate transfer to a former spouse fail at the transferor's death, and community property rules can split a policy bought during marriage, so the clean 'pay Maria' answer is not reliable for California.
excluded.LH-HPRV-001: Says a monthly-premium individual health policy has a 10-day grace period. California individual health benefit plans must allow at least 30 days (3 months for subsidized enrollees) before termination for nonpayment (Ins. Code 10273.6), so the key is wrong for ACA major medical in California.
